baseline_items.text:
RE-call's DB-backed suite produces failures that have nothing to do with the code under test,
repeatedly and at wildly different scales: 15 failed + 5 errors, 473 errors, 41 failed + 59
errors, 8 failed + 12 errors, and single one-off errors. Every one passed on isolated re-run.
Budget for it: the full suite is 15-20 minutes, so a false red is expensive to chase.

so an unconfigured run skips loudly instead of silently sharing a database. The manual `docker
run` recipe below is now `scripts/session-db.sh`:

⚠️ **The exception, and only this one: a single DB-free FILE.** 2026-08-15 a reachable but
schema-incompatible database made `conftest.py`'s session-scoped autouse
`_bootstrap_default_test_schema` raise out of `apply_migrations`, which **ERRORed every test in the
repo**, including files that touch no database. An untouched file errored identically, which is how

**Before adding any guard that inspects the database role's privileges, know that the suite's
default role is the cluster superuser.** `docker-compose.yml` ships `POSTGRES_USER=recall` and that
role owns the cluster; CI's `pgvector/pgvector` service container does the same. So a guard that
refuses privileged roles refuses the entire test environment.

⛔ **Never "isolate" a DB-free change by pointing the DSN at a dead port.** `_db_available()`
covers most of the suite but not all: three `tests/test_bench_systems.py::test_recall_system_*`
tests FAIL with `psycopg.errors.ConnectionTimeout` instead of skipping, manufacturing a red that
looks like your change.

That is safe for a file with no DB tests and stays wrong for a sweep, for the reason above: the
`test_bench_systems.py::test_recall_system_*` trio fails rather than skips. **ERRORs everywhere,
including in files you did not touch, means fixture or collection breakage, never your diff.**

**Assert the DB is reachable before the sweep**, rather than inferring it after, one
`psycopg.connect(..., connect_timeout=5)` whose failure is unambiguous.

⛔ **Bind `127.0.0.1` explicitly and pick a free port.** Port 5432 on this machine has had TWO
listeners: a docker container on `0.0.0.0:5432` and a native Postgres on `[::1]:5432`. Windows
resolves `localhost` to `::1` first, so the default `RECALL_TEST_DSN`
(`...@localhost:5432/recall`) can reach a different database than the docker one you think you are
testing. That is not contention; it is two databases wearing one name, and it explains reds that
isolation alone does not. The 2026-08-14 prune mattered for exactly this reason and not for the
458.8 kB it reclaimed: TEN of those containers claimed `0.0.0.0:5432`, and whichever started first
won silently. Prune the exited ones when the list gets long.

`_UNCONFIGURED_DSN` pointed at port 1, and the docstring justifying the whole design said every
connection there "is refused immediately, on any platform" and that "the worst outcome is a
confusing connection error". Measured on this host:

| probe | actual |
| --- | --- |
| socket to 127.0.0.1:1 | refused after **2.03 s** |
| socket to 127.0.0.1:5999 (also closed) | refused after **2.01 s** |
| `psycopg.connect(port-1 DSN)`, no `connect_timeout` | **130 s** stall |

The delay is a property of this Windows host, not of port 1, so a different port would not have
helped. `tests/` has ~110 `psycopg.connect(TEST_DSN...)` sites that pass no timeout. Fixed by
putting `?connect_timeout=2` in the constant, so the bound cannot be forgotten per call site.

## When it comes back red

**1. Read the SKIP count before the pass count.** 2026-08-14: `3 failed, 3763 passed, 514
skipped` reads as nearly green. It was not a test result. Docker was still starting, the DSN
pointed at nothing, two thirds of the suite skipped, and the three failures were the
`test_recall_system_*` trio above. **22 skipped is healthy here; 514 means the database was never
reached.** The pass count cannot show that, because the tests that would have failed never ran.

**2. Count the competition.** One cheap command that reframes everything downstream:

powershell -NoProfile -Command "Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter \"Name='python.exe'\" | Select-Object ProcessId,CommandLine"

- ⚠️ **Ogni pytest locale va prefissato** con `RECALL_TEST_DSN="postgresql://recall:recall@localhost:1/recall"`.
  Questa macchina ha un DB raggiungibile con schema incompatibile (`vector(384)` vs `dim=64`) e
  la fixture autouse di sessione fa morire l'intera suite con migliaia di errori. Con la porta
  morta, `_db_available()` è False e la fixture prende il **suo** ramo no-op già progettato.
  ⛔ Non "risolverlo" con un `tests/fleet/conftest.py`: provato e revertito, committa un override
  permanente per rimediare all'ambiente di una macchina.
- `docs/superpowers/` è **gitignored** in RE-call: gli spec versionati stanno in `docs/*_DESIGN.md`.
- La fleet non tocca nessun DB: `QueryKeyedStore` è duck-typed e `_score_config` riceve lo store.

## Debito lasciato

🔑 **The mechanism, in one line:** `tests/conftest.py` decided "is there a database" by opening a
connection with `connect_timeout=2`, and `require_db()` called it **per test**, uncached. On a
loaded host a probe loses that race, and `require_db()` responds to a lost race by **skipping**.

⛔ **This is a false GREEN, which is why it survived.** A flake that produces a red gets chased. A
flake that produces a skip produces a passing run, and the only trace is a skip count nobody
compares between runs. `CLAUDE.md` already warned "read the skip count before calling a run green"
and named several hundred as the danger signal; 88 against 34 is well under that and still lost a
quarter of the database coverage.

- **The test suite must never point at it.** It is a corpus, not a scratch database.

⚠️ **Do not attribute such a failure to the parallel isolation without checking.** In the same run,
six other failures were genuinely mine (a DSN rewritten into libpq keyword form) and ten were a
real cross-worker collision (a module-scoped fixed-name database). Three causes, one red run, and
they need different fixes. See [[test-suite-runs-in-parallel-now]] and
[[concurrent-pytest-false-reds]], which already listed pool assertions as CPU-contention-sensitive
and would have predicted this one.

**Why it costs more than it should:** the error names a schema, not a cause, and it fires on tests
that have nothing to do with the script. The first time I read it as a defect in the test file I
had just written.

**How to apply.** Either give a measurement its own database, or reset between:

```bash
bash scripts/session-db.sh down && bash scripts/session-db.sh up
```

Two seconds, and it puts the container back where conftest expects it. Prefer resetting **after**
the measurement rather than before the suite, so the wrong state never outlives the run that
created it.

2026-08-26 (#518). I made an RLS-bypassing role **fatal** for authenticated multi-tenant serving in
`recall_mcp/server.py` (`require_effective_rls`). It broke **9 tests** across
`tests/test_mcp_auth_http.py` and `tests/test_rate_limit_http.py`. Both spawn a real
`streamable-http` server with authentication — exactly the multi-tenant case the guard refuses —
with `"RECALL_DSN": TEST_DSN`. Every one failed at fixture setup with my own error message and
`ERROR: Application startup failed`.

**This would have been a red CI, and only running the suite found it.** `ruff`, `mypy`, the targeted
tests for the change itself and its five new unit tests were all green, because the guard's own tests
call a pure function and never stand up a server.

## The fix is `unprivileged_dsn`, not an exemption

This does **not** retire what follows. The port-1 default removes the *silent sharing* failure;
it does nothing about a quiet machine, foreign pytest processes, `tmp_path` pruning, or the
`::1` versus `0.0.0.0` split on 5432. Keep reading the skip count first.

## Before you run anything

**Start your own container.** There is no standing one to reuse. Through 2026-08-13 a
`recall-suite-db` sat on `127.0.0.1:55432` and this note said to reuse it; on 2026-08-14 the
container list had reached 26 leftovers and `docker container prune` removed all 25 stopped ones,
that among them. (Volumes survive a container prune, so 97 dangling volumes still hold the data,
but reattaching by hex id is not worth it.)

**Prefer impossible over detectable.** A static guard proving every DB test carried `@requires_db`
was wrong three times, each caught by an auditor: it hid 161 of 363 tests behind wrapper fixtures,
then 17 more, then misclassified 227 locals, always green while the property went unchecked over
a growing share of the suite, because I derived truth from a hand-written list and kept widening
it. Making `make_store` call `pytest.skip()` deleted 574 lines of inference, is exact rather than
approximate, and protects the tests whose author forgot the mark, the entire population at risk.
Ask early: can I make this impossible instead of detectable?

1. Every xdist worker is a separate process and pays collection AGAIN, so a module-scope import of
   a 75s dependency is multiplied rather than amortised. The four tests that need the SDK take a
   session-scoped `voyageai_sdk` fixture now.
2. Workers share one database. `tests/conftest.py::_isolate_xdist_worker` gives each its own.
   ⚠️ **It rewrites the DSN as a URL, never through `psycopg.conninfo.make_conninfo`.** Keyword
   form is valid libpq and psycopg accepts it, but five tests take `TEST_DSN` apart with
   `urlsplit` or `rsplit("/", 1)`, and keyword form made all five fail while naming their own
   string handling. That cost one 17-minute run to find.

🔴 **2026-08-14: I read this rule, then ignored it three times, and the user caught it.** A
`recall-suite-db` was up on 55432 and I used it for three full-suite runs without asking whose it
was. It was another session's. Mid-session it was REMOVED, so by the time the user asked "check
the container is yours" the port was dead and the next run would have skipped every DB test while
reporting green. One of those three runs produced the 4258-pass figure that went into a MERGED
PR's description: it happened to be honest (22 skipped, so the DB was reached), but it shared a
database with a session that could have been writing to it, and I had no way to know.

The fix is a session-scoped `tmp_path_factory.mktemp(...)` handed to the autouse fixture, so the
suite-wide default lives outside every test's scratch space. Session scope is safe when the writes
are uuid-keyed; a per-test directory under the factory root is the alternative if they are not.

**Why:** a suite-wide fixture is invisible at the failure site, so the debugging starts in the wrong
file. The two tests above read as flaky or as regressions in `apply_proposal` and the LOCOMO walk.

# Typed relation coverage in PR 620

PR 620 now carries safe ingestion for authored `supports`, `contradicts`,
`depends_on`, `caused`, and `same_entity` relations. Inferred relations remain
exploratory candidates and cannot become trusted evidence. Relation coverage
and per relation seed, acceptance, and trusted evidence telemetry are reported.

Commits `05e7cda5` and `92810589` are pushed on `codex/graph-reasoning`. The
focused graph, reasoning, evaluation, projection, and database suite passed 81
tests, and the related database probe coverage passed 20 tests. The persistent
development database migration ledger is aligned through migration 0024.

Measured 2026-08-21 on PR #452. Locally: **6279 passed, 34 skipped, ruff clean**, full suite against
a real database, 36 minutes. On CI: **4 checks red**. Nothing was flaky; every failure was real and
every one was mine.

- [Two stores for one credential must share a key](two-stores-for-one-credential-must-share-a-key.md) — one keyed by account and one not is a silent cross-account leak; a suite with only one identity can never see it.

🔑 **The `lme_s` index is the valuable part: it cost 6h39m of bge-small embedding, and it is why
further arms are ~15 min instead of 8h.** A reranker arm, a voyage-3 comparison or a recalibration
all just re-read it. `Indexer` skips by content hash, so re-running the index over the same corpus
is a no-op rather than a re-embed.

⚠️ **Port 5432 on VPS2 is the LIVE Postgres.** The container is deliberately remapped to 5533 and
bound to loopback; the live `sentiment_agent` DB was never touched. Run the test suite against
`RECALL_TEST_DSN=…:5533/recall_test`, never the `recall` DB — the suite drops tables and would
destroy `lme_s`.

Observed 2026-08-23 in the recall worktree. A full test suite launched as a harness background
task "completed (exit code 0)" after ~10 minutes with an output file containing only
`[exited with code 0]`, no pytest output at all. The process was still alive (found later by
`Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` matching the exact command line) and kept writing to a database.
Trusting the notification and relaunching produced TWO concurrent suites against one session DB,
whose global-table tests interfere; both had to be killed and one clean run started.

query.query: can two pytest sessions run at the same time here

baseline_items.text:
Two pytest sessions running at the same time against the same test database collide. `tests/conftest.py`
calls `apply_migrations` from a session fixture, and `recall.schema`'s guard refuses the second one:

recall.schema.ConcurrentMigrator: another RE-call schema migrator is already running

The loser does not fail one test. **Every** test errors at setup, so the run reports e.g.
`3 skipped, 62 errors` with no failures at all. Reproduced deliberately on 2026-08-05 with three
concurrent runs of `tests/test_bench_systems.py`: one passed, two errored wholesale.

**How to apply:**
1. A suite verdict is the SUMMARY LINE, never an exit code. An output file with no pytest output
   means "did not run or was lost", whatever the code says.
2. Launch long suites detached with their own log (`nohup python -u -m pytest tests/ -q > log
   2>&1 &`, the `-u` matters or the log stays empty for minutes) and watch the log with a
   Monitor until-loop for the summary line.
3. Before relaunching anything DB-backed, list live python processes and match COMMAND LINES:
   two suites on one session database invalidate each other silently.
4. Distinguish your processes from other sessions' by command line before killing: this machine
   routinely runs parallel sessions with their own suites.

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `ConcurrentMigrator` in fixture setup | two pytest processes contend for the schema-migration advisory lock; `scripts/ablate_store_latency_guards.py` documents it |
| `LockNotAvailable: canceling statement due to lock timeout` | another session on the SAME container, still running |
| `test_rate_limit_http.py`, `test_mcp_auth_http.py` | these stand up real HTTP servers and contend on PORTS; a private container does not protect them |
| `FileNotFoundError` inside `tmp_path` | pytest keeps only the 3 most recent `pytest-of-<user>/pytest-<n>` roots and prunes older ones AT STARTUP, so a new run deletes the dirs of runs in flight |
| pool / latency / backend-count assertions ("pool churned: 3 distinct backends…") | CPU contention, not DB contention |
|

**Why it matters:** the guard is working as designed, but its failure signature looks exactly like a
catastrophic breakage of the code under test. It cost me a wrong conclusion once: in a mutation-testing
harness I counted two mutants as "caught" because the suite went red, when the redness was this
collision and not the mutant.

**How to apply:** run pytest sessions in this repo **sequentially**, never overlapping. In any harness
that shells out to pytest in a loop, treat `errors` and `failed` as different evidence: only `failed`
means a test caught something. Retry (or abort) on seeing `ConcurrentMigrator` in the output rather
than scoring that run. See also [[bench-systems-suite-spends-openrouter-credits]] for the other trap in
this same file.

---

🔑 **The competing process is usually one I started myself.** A `bug-auditor` subagent runs pytest.
Chaining `pytest A && pytest B` overlaps if the first has not fully released its connections. Both
happened repeatedly, and I diagnosed the results as broken apparatus, code regression, catalog
bloat and machine contention before noticing I was the other party. **Tell subagents explicitly not
to touch the database, and never run a suite while one is live.**

🔑 **The failing test set CHANGES every run** and each one passes in isolation, which reads exactly
like order-dependent shared state. There is no randomiser installed — it is whichever test happened
to be migrating when the lock was taken.

**How to apply.** Never gate on `claude -p`'s exit status; grep its output for the expected content
and treat absence as failure. Better, avoid it entirely for measurement: a session's own MCP tool

baseline.text:
Two pytest sessions running at the same time against the same test database collide. `tests/conftest.py`
calls `apply_migrations` from a session fixture, and `recall.schema`'s guard refuses the second one:

recall.schema.ConcurrentMigrator: another RE-call schema migrator is already running

The loser does not fail one test. **Every** test errors at setup, so the run reports e.g.
`3 skipped, 62 errors` with no failures at all. Reproduced deliberately on 2026-08-05 with three
concurrent runs of `tests/test_bench_systems.py`: one passed, two errored wholesale.

**How to apply:**
1. A suite verdict is the SUMMARY LINE, never an exit code. An output file with no pytest output
   means "did not run or was lost", whatever the code says.
2. Launch long suites detached with their own log (`nohup python -u -m pytest tests/ -q > log
   2>&1 &`, the `-u` matters or the log stays empty for minutes) and watch the log with a
   Monitor until-loop for the summary line.
3. Before relaunching anything DB-backed, list live python processes and match COMMAND LINES:
   two suites on one session database invalidate each other silently.
4. Distinguish your processes from other sessions' by command line before killing: this machine
   routinely runs parallel sessions with their own suites.

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `ConcurrentMigrator` in fixture setup | two pytest processes contend for the schema-migration advisory lock; `scripts/ablate_store_latency_guards.py` documents it |
| `LockNotAvailable: canceling statement due to lock timeout` | another session on the SAME container, still running |
| `test_rate_limit_http.py`, `test_mcp_auth_http.py` | these stand up real HTTP servers and contend on PORTS; a private container does not protect them |
| `FileNotFoundError` inside `tmp_path` | pytest keeps only the 3 most recent `pytest-of-<user>/pytest-<n>` roots and prunes older ones AT STARTUP, so a new run deletes the dirs of runs in flight |
| pool / latency / backend-count assertions ("pool churned: 3 distinct backends…") | CPU contention, not DB contention |
|

**Why it matters:** the guard is working as designed, but its failure signature looks exactly like a
catastrophic breakage of the code under test. It cost me a wrong conclusion once: in a mutation-testing
harness I counted two mutants as "caught" because the suite went red, when the redness was this
collision and not the mutant.

**How to apply:** run pytest sessions in this repo **sequentially**, never overlapping. In any harness
that shells out to pytest in a loop, treat `errors` and `failed` as different evidence: only `failed`
means a test caught something. Retry (or abort) on seeing `ConcurrentMigrator` in the output rather
than scoring that run. See also [[bench-systems-suite-spends-openrouter-credits]] for the other trap in
this same file.

query.query: how long does the full test suite take with a database
query.label_note: The legacy relevant_ids are retained for historical comparability, but their source is superseded by this live successor.

baseline_items.text:
**Measured 2026-08-18** on this Windows workstation, with a session container:

```
5694 passed, 32 skipped in 1857.08s (0:30:57)
```

`CLAUDE.md:140` states "The full suite takes about **12 minutes** with a database and about 5
without." That is **stale by a factor of two and a half**, and it is a claim in a file loaded into
every session, so it is believed by default.

## Why it matters beyond the number

A 15 or 20 minute timeout looks generous against the documented figure and **kills the run at
roughly two thirds**. That is exactly what happened here on the first attempt, and the killed run
then reported success because its exit code came from a `| tail` rather than from pytest. Two
independent defects lined up to turn "the suite did not finish" into "the suite passed".

RE-call's DB-backed suite produces failures that have nothing to do with the code under test,
repeatedly and at wildly different scales: 15 failed + 5 errors, 473 errors, 41 failed + 59
errors, 8 failed + 12 errors, and single one-off errors. Every one passed on isolated re-run.
Budget for it: the full suite is 15-20 minutes, so a false red is expensive to chase.

## 2026-08-15: the root cause is fixed in the repo. Use the scripts.

`tests/conftest.py` no longer defaults to `localhost:5432`. Unset, `TEST_DSN` points at port 1,
so an unconfigured run skips loudly instead of silently sharing a database. The manual `docker
run` recipe below is now `scripts/session-db.sh`:

— read before adding any guard keyed on database privilege. `docker-compose.yml` and CI both hand the suite a superuser, so an RLS guard broke 9 HTTP-server tests; `conftest.unprivileged_dsn` already exists for it.
- [Fastembed is not why the suite is slow](fastembed-is-not-why-the-suite-is-slow.md) — measured 2026-08-26: all real-model tests are 73 tests / 80s; >40 min runs mean serial or a loaded box, and make test now preflights via scripts/suite-preflight.sh.
- [agent-memory-bench site: live](agent-memory-bench-site-2026-08-26.md) — read BEFORE editing any page there: the public site names NO third-party product and a test enforces it, while the harness still runs all eight arms under their real names. Deployed at giulioder.github.io/agent-memory-bench; leaderboard.js is generated

⛔ **Never "isolate" a DB-free change by pointing the DSN at a dead port.** `_db_available()`
covers most of the suite but not all: three `tests/test_bench_systems.py::test_recall_system_*`

trimmed. And before restarting anything long, check liveness by process and CPU, because a restart
under contention costs the whole elapsed run and lands in the same queue.

query.query: what happens if I mix two embedding models in one tenant

baseline_items.text:
🔑 **One embedding model per tenant.** Not a convention: it is the only thing standing between a
mixed corpus and silently wrong retrieval. When a corpus wants a code model and a prose model,
that is two tenants, not one with two writers.

Found on 2026-08-15 designing the `recall_repos` corpus on VPS2 (five repositories, code via
`voyage-code-3`, docs via `voyage-4`). Ten tenants, `<repo>-code` and `<repo>-docs`, for exactly
this reason. The index driver asserts `code_embedder.dim == docs_embedder.dim` before writing,
because both tenants share one table and one fixed vector width.

⚠️ The same reasoning applies to the CHUNKER, but the failure is different and worse: see
[[chunker-is-not-in-the-index-fingerprint]]. Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]],
[[recall-corpus-name-boundary]].

`RetrievalDiagnostics.embedding_profile` (`recall/retriever.py:325`, `:471`) is **reported, never
enforced**. Nothing in `recall/store.py` filters rows by it: the only occurrence is a `count(*)
FILTER (WHERE NOT metadata ? 'embedding_profile')` used for a readiness report. So a tenant holding
passages from two models is not an error state the code can see.

It is also not a *loud* failure, which is the part that matters. pgvector would reject a dimension
mismatch, so two models of DIFFERENT width fail fast. The dangerous case is two models of the
**same** width: `voyage-4` and `voyage-code-3` are both 1024, so a query embedded with one is
cosine-compared against passages embedded with the other, the SQL succeeds, and the ranking is
garbage that looks exactly like a ranking.

🔑 **Verify an embedder by `vector_dims(embedding)`, never by the profile label**: at least on
the fastembed path. Extends [[mixing-embedders-in-one-tenant-is-silent]]: the field that was
supposed to make mixing detectable is itself inert, so that lesson is stronger than written.

Not filed as a fix yet. The fix is to derive the default `profile_id` from model name plus
dimension, which re-fingerprints every fastembed corpus, a migration, not a one-liner.

So a live memory search embeds the query with voyage-4 and compares it against 8,716 bge-small
document vectors. **Both models emit 1024 dimensions, so pgvector computes a cosine happily** and
returns a confidently ranked list that means nothing. No error, no warning, no failure code that
names it.

Re-measure (the profile lives in the row's metadata, and mixing shows up as more than one value):

```bash
psql "$RECALL_DSN" -c "SELECT tenant_id, metadata->>'embedding_profile' AS profile, count(*) \
  FROM chunks GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,3 DESC;"
ssh vps2 "ps -eo args | grep -o 'RECALL_TENANT=[^ ]* RECALL_EMBEDDER=[^ ]*' | sort -u"
```

reported
`corpus: 9552 chunks, 0 of them keyed by a Windows path`, so the adoption held across a day and
a further sync. The hazard is closed; this memo is now about the MECHANISM, which recurs
wherever a corpus moves hosts, rather than about an open task.

**The tenant's other defect was fixed in the same session, in the other direction from the one this
memo assumed.** It held two profiles at once (6,392 `bge-small-symmetric-v1`, 3,060 bge-large) while
the client queried it with `voyage-4`, so the corpus was re-embedded with **voyage-4** rather than
the client being pointed at bge-large: the sibling tenants already use it, and the alternative puts
a 1.4 GB ONNX model inside every stdio server session on that host. See
[[vps2-memory-tenant-mixes-three-embedders]].

Not filed as a fix yet. The fix is to derive the default `profile_id` from model name plus
dimension, which re-fingerprints every fastembed corpus, a migration, not a one-liner.

So a live memory search embeds the query with voyage-4 and compares it against 8,716 bge-small
document vectors. **Both models emit 1024 dimensions, so pgvector computes a cosine happily** and
returns a confidently ranked list that means nothing. No error, no warning, no failure code that
names it.

Re-measure (the profile lives in the row's metadata, and mixing shows up as more than one value):

```bash
psql "$RECALL_DSN" -c "SELECT tenant_id, metadata->>'embedding_profile' AS profile, count(*) \
  FROM chunks GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,3 DESC;"
ssh vps2 "ps -eo args | grep -o 'RECALL_TENANT=[^ ]* RECALL_EMBEDDER=[^ ]*' | sort -u"
```

reported
`corpus: 9552 chunks, 0 of them keyed by a Windows path`, so the adoption held across a day and
a further sync. The hazard is closed; this memo is now about the MECHANISM, which recurs
wherever a corpus moves hosts, rather than about an open task.

**The tenant's other defect was fixed in the same session, in the other direction from the one this
memo assumed.** It held two profiles at once (6,392 `bge-small-symmetric-v1`, 3,060 bge-large) while
the client queried it with `voyage-4`, so the corpus was re-embedded with **voyage-4** rather than
the client being pointed at bge-large: the sibling tenants already use it, and the alternative puts
a 1.4 GB ONNX model inside every stdio server session on that host. See
[[vps2-memory-tenant-mixes-three-embedders]].

🔑 **One embedding model per tenant.** Not a convention: it is the only thing standing between a
mixed corpus and silently wrong retrieval. When a corpus wants a code model and a prose model,
that is two tenants, not one with two writers.

Found on 2026-08-15 designing the `recall_repos` corpus on VPS2 (five repositories, code via
`voyage-code-3`, docs via `voyage-4`). Ten tenants, `<repo>-code` and `<repo>-docs`, for exactly
this reason. The index driver asserts `code_embedder.dim == docs_embedder.dim` before writing,
because both tenants share one table and one fixed vector width.

⚠️ The same reasoning applies to the CHUNKER, but the failure is different and worse: see
[[chunker-is-not-in-the-index-fingerprint]]. Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]],
[[recall-corpus-name-boundary]].

`RetrievalDiagnostics.embedding_profile` (`recall/retriever.py:325`, `:471`) is **reported, never
enforced**. Nothing in `recall/store.py` filters rows by it: the only occurrence is a `count(*)
FILTER (WHERE NOT metadata ? 'embedding_profile')` used for a readiness report. So a tenant holding
passages from two models is not an error state the code can see.

It is also not a *loud* failure, which is the part that matters. pgvector would reject a dimension
mismatch, so two models of DIFFERENT width fail fast. The dangerous case is two models of the
**same** width: `voyage-4` and `voyage-code-3` are both 1024, so a query embedded with one is
cosine-compared against passages embedded with the other, the SQL succeeds, and the ranking is
garbage that looks exactly like a ranking.

Related: [[mixing-embedders-in-one-tenant-is-silent]], [[no-pinned-revision-for-the-default-embedder]],
[[calibrated-thresholds-and-the-overlap]].

Measured 2026-08-20 on `recall_repos` (VPS2, port 55432) and from `ps` on that host.

**Three different embedding models are in play on one tenant, and every layer is silent about it.**

| where | model | rows |
|---|---|---|
| live MCP server's query embedder (`RECALL_EMBEDDER`) | `voyage:voyage-4` | n/a |
| legacy `chunks`, which that server reads | `bge-small-symmetric-v1` | **8,716** |
| same table, written 2026-08-19 | `voyage:voyage-4` | 2 |
| `recall_chunks_v1` generation, which the calibration binds to | **bge-large** | 8,671 |

⛔ **This is fatal, not merely suboptimal.** Own measurement, 2026-08-17: `voyage-4` scored
0.269–0.413 on a corpus where `voyage-code-3` scored 0.480–0.834, recorded in
[[calibrated-thresholds-and-the-overlap]] as "'Voyage' is not an embedder; a threshold binds to the
exact model." Cosines from different models are not on one scale, so neither ranking nor threshold
survives the mix.

**Cost of not knowing:** a calibration was measured and published on 2026-08-18 against the
bge-large generation, and it was inert, because the serving path read a different table built with
a different model and queried it with a third. Diagnosing "the corpus went stale" would have fixed
nothing.

## Two consequences measured 2026-08-18

Measured 2026-08-19, in recall's own memory corpus, using recall itself.

A memo carried a 🔁 correction at the top of the file retracting a claim in its middle. Searching
for that claim returned **the falsified paragraph on its own**, as chunk ordinal 7, with no trace of
the correction: retrieval returns **chunks**, and the correction was in a different one.

The second attempt failed too, and this is the part worth keeping. I inserted a ⛔ retraction
paragraph **immediately above** the falsified block, re-indexed, and re-ran the query. The chunker
does not split on paragraph boundaries, so the retraction landed in the neighbouring chunk again and
the claim still came back naked.

So a crash does **not** mean nothing was indexed. `recall` (208 memos) completed and its new memos
were confirmed findable by a real search; `sentiment-agent` (987 memos) is the one that blew up and
whose server mirror is now stale with nothing reporting the gap. Read the per-project lines before
concluding the whole sync failed, and before re-running the whole thing.

⚠️ **Do not "fix" it by indexing only the failing project.** Re-indexing prunes files absent from the
slice, and `--allow-prune` gates only a MASSIVE prune, so a small one happens silently. The protocol
says this and it is the one part of that section still correct.

policy) or delete the affected sources first and let the next run re-read them.

The source docstring calls widening the tuple out as a migration rather than a comment change,
because it re-fingerprints every indexed corpus at once. That is a real cost and the reason it has
not been done, not an oversight.

Found on 2026-08-15 fixing `recall index`, which chose the chunker from the GLOB SUFFIX
(`chunk_code if args.glob.endswith(".py") else chunk_text`) rather than per file, so
`--glob '**/*'` chunked every `.py` as prose and said nothing. Fixed by `chunker_for_path`, with
the non-repair noted in its docstring so the next person does not assume a re-index is enough.

⚠️ `chunk_code` is **Python-specific**: it starts a block at a column-0 `def`/`class`/`@`/`async
def`. Given Rust, SQL or shell it matches nothing, returns one block, and is strictly worse than
`chunk_text`, which at least splits on blank lines. Do not widen `PYTHON_SUFFIXES` without a
chunker that parses the language being added.

## Two consequences measured 2026-08-18

Measured 2026-08-19, in recall's own memory corpus, using recall itself.

A memo carried a 🔁 correction at the top of the file retracting a claim in its middle. Searching
for that claim returned **the falsified paragraph on its own**, as chunk ordinal 7, with no trace of
the correction: retrieval returns **chunks**, and the correction was in a different one.

The second attempt failed too, and this is the part worth keeping. I inserted a ⛔ retraction
paragraph **immediately above** the falsified block, re-indexed, and re-ran the query. The chunker
does not split on paragraph boundaries, so the retraction landed in the neighbouring chunk again and
the claim still came back naked.

🔑 **A corpus can hold chunks from SEVERAL chunker eras at once, and that is the NORMAL result of
any chunker change, not an exotic case.** It follows directly from the omission above: the run after
the change skips every unchanged file, so those keep their old chunking while newly changed files
get the new one. Anything that must assert one `ChunkerIdentity` for a whole corpus (a generation's
`PipelineIdentity` carries exactly one) therefore cannot assume homogeneity. Check per source.

✅ **The chunker IS recoverable from the stored chunks, cheaply.** Nothing records it, but
re-deriving the body with `parse_frontmatter` and re-chunking with a candidate configuration
reproduces the stored chunk list exactly when the candidate is right. Measured over the `memory`
corpus, 1,058 usable sources: `chunk_text(max_chars=800, overlap=80)` reproduced **1,058 of 1,058**,
while `overlap=0` got 535, `chunk_text(1200,80)` 43 and `chunk_code(800)` 31. **0.16 s for a full
pass**, so this is exhaustive rather than sampled.

## A third way to be green locally and red in CI, hit 2026-08-29 on PR #18

The version was right and the command was still wrong: I ran `python -m ruff check` on **each file
as I wrote it** and never on the tree. CI runs `ruff check .` and failed with five findings, all in
one new test file, none of which the per-file runs had covered because I never pointed one at that
file.

⛔ **The argument to `ruff check` is part of the command. `python -m ruff check adapters/foo/` is
not a weaker version of the CI check, it is a different check.** Same failure family as the version
gap above and as [[windows-dev-linux-ci-hides-defects-in-both-directions]]: something that looked
like the CI command and was not.

Run the whole thing before pushing, which is also cheap:

```bash

**How to apply:** before trusting a scoped check, **print what the scope matched** (`| wc -l`,
`--name-only`). And run the verification command the *gate* runs, not a convenient subset of it —
if CI runs `ruff check .`, run `ruff check .`. A narrower check than the gate is not a check.

itself the defect — pin it, and run that pinned version locally (a throwaway venv is enough).
"Same command" is not "same answer".

produced the single best finding of the run — a test guarding "the label must never be a lie" that
passed vacuously, proven by mutation. The gap was worth closing, not noting.

baseline_items.text:
RE-call has never been run through `ruff format`. As of 2026-08-08, `python -m ruff format --check .`
reports **348 of 406 files would be reformatted**. CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs only
`ruff check .` plus bare `mypy`. `pyproject.toml` sets `[tool.ruff] line-length = 100` and nothing
else about formatting.

**Why:** a `ruff format --check` failure on a file I am touching looks like a defect I introduced or
a nit worth clearing. It is neither. It is the repo's baseline state. I flagged one as a nit and
"fixed" it, which imposed an unused convention on one arbitrary file and put two unrelated hunks
into a diff that was supposed to be eight lines of test markers.

**How to apply:** run `python -m ruff check` to gate my work, never `ruff format`. If a format
failure appears on a file I edited, confirm it predates me (`git stash` then re-check) and leave it.
Reformatting is a repo-wide decision for the user, not a side effect of an unrelated change.

Related: [[ruff-blocked-locally]] for why it must be `python -m ruff` and not bare `ruff`.

query.query: what happens to a project's memory when I rename its directory

baseline_items.text:
- **Before renaming a project directory**, move `~/.claude/projects/<old-slug>/memory/` into the new
  slug. Do it at rename time; there is no later signal that anything is missing.
- **When a memory store looks thin for a project with history**, list `~/.claude/projects/` and look
  for a slug matching an old name of the directory. Two stores for one project is the tell.
- The same key derivation strands stores when a **user profile** changes: 533 memos under
  `C--Users-temen-*` belong to a Windows profile that no longer exists.

Archived, not deleted, at `~/.claude/archive/stranded-memory-stores-2026-08-15/`, with a README
recording what was recovered and what was deliberately left unmerged.

`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/` is keyed on the **project path**. Rename the directory and a

Corollary worth carrying: the entry is keyed by path at all, so **moving or renaming the project
orphans whatever is under it**, silently. Same shape as the memory-store forking described in
`CLAUDE.md`. Re-run the installer after a move, and print the key that was registered.

**Why it costs something.** Anything written *under* a project key is invisible to a launch using
the other spelling, with no error: right file, right shape, wrong key, silent nothing. That is the
same failure class as [[mcp-servers-blocked-by-pending-approval]], reached by a different route,
and it is the reason recall's wizard writes **every existing key that resolves to the project
directory** rather than one invented one (`_project_keys` in `recall/wizard/wiring.py`). A key is
invented only when the client has none, which means the user has never opened that project.

Compare keys **resolved**, never as strings. `Path(key).resolve() == project_root.resolve()` treats
the two spellings above as one directory; `==` on the strings does not.

## ⛔ The scores are not results, and I got this wrong first

`recall/desktop/runtime.py` runs `docker compose up -d --wait` and passes `-p` **only** when
`profile.compose_project` is set. The shipped desktop profile does not set it, so Compose falls
back to naming the project after the **directory**, which in a worktree is the worktree's name.
That is the mechanism behind `<worktree>-recall-docs-1` and friends, and it is why three other
worktrees on this machine carry the same set.

⚠️ **I did not establish which code path started mine**, only that the containers carried
`com.docker.compose.project.working_dir` pointing at my worktree and appeared during a full-suite
run. Do not repeat the guess as a fact; if it matters, catch it with `docker events` during a run.

So a crash does **not** mean nothing was indexed. `recall` (208 memos) completed and its new memos
were confirmed findable by a real search; `sentiment-agent` (987 memos) is the one that blew up and
whose server mirror is now stale with nothing reporting the gap. Read the per-project lines before
concluding the whole sync failed, and before re-running the whole thing.

⚠️ **Do not "fix" it by indexing only the failing project.** Re-indexing prunes files absent from the
slice, and `--allow-prune` gates only a MASSIVE prune, so a small one happens silently. The protocol
says this and it is the one part of that section still correct.

**The memory corpus maintains itself now. One command for a session, a scheduled task for
everything else.** Built 2026-08-27 at the user's request ("one command that runs all the phases;
add the memo to the folder and the system runs everything on its own"), on top of the manifest
pipeline that landed the day before ([[vps2-memory-index-goes-through-the-manifest-pipeline]]).

```

**Why it costs something.** Anything written *under* a project key is invisible to a launch using
the other spelling, with no error: right file, right shape, wrong key, silent nothing. That is the
same failure class as [[mcp-servers-blocked-by-pending-approval]], reached by a different route,
and it is the reason recall's wizard writes **every existing key that resolves to the project
directory** rather than one invented one (`_project_keys` in `recall/wizard/wiring.py`). A key is
invented only when the client has none, which means the user has never opened that project.

Compare keys **resolved**, never as strings. `Path(key).resolve() == project_root.resolve()` treats
the two spellings above as one directory; `==` on the strings does not.

**Claude Code keys `projects` in `~/.claude.json` by whatever path string it was launched with, and
does not normalise it.** One directory can therefore hold several entries.

Measured **2026-08-19**, against the real config, **313 project keys**. The same directory appeared
as both:

```
'C:\\Users\\gde00\\Documents\\progetto sentimental'
'C:/Users/gde00/Documents/progetto sentimental'
```

A native Windows launch and a Git Bash launch produce different spellings of one path.

Re-measure:

```bash
python -c "import json,os;d=json.load(open(os.path.expanduser('~/.claude.json')));ks=list(d['projects']);print(len(ks));[print(repr(k)) for k in ks[:6]]"
```

pipe a command whose exit status gates a `&&` chain; capture the status explicitly instead. And
check the target worktree is clean before merging into it.

```
# 1. build complete bundle with refs/heads/master (master branch may be locked by another worktree,

git fetch origin master

git -C /tmp/b.git bundle create master.bundle master   # ref = refs/heads/master
# 2. VPS2: scp master.bundle → /tmp (chmod 644); then as qwen:
sudo -u qwen git -C /var/lib/qwen_agent/repo fetch /tmp/master.bundle

**How to apply:** ancestry against `HEAD` is never evidence about master. Ask the question that
matters, at the START and again before merging, and read it as a supersession signal:

git log --oneline HEAD..master -- <the files you are about to touch>

Any output means someone changed those files ahead of you. `git merge-tree $(git merge-base HEAD
master) HEAD master | grep "changed in both"` confirms it in one more command. And when a commit is
"not an ancestor", the next command is `git branch -a --contains <sha>` INCLUDING master, not a
conclusion.

**Why this bit me:** I ran `git checkout master 2>&1 | tail -2 && git merge --squash <branch>`. The
pipe made `&&` read `tail`'s exit status, not the failed checkout's, so the squash merge ran against
the *feature branch* that happened to be checked out, leaving 13 staged additions and two
conflicted files in the user's working tree. `git reset --hard HEAD` restored it because nothing was
committed and the tree had been clean.

**How to apply:** Check `git worktree list` before assuming any branch can be checked out. Never
pipe a command whose exit status gates a `&&` chain; capture the status explicitly instead. And
check the target worktree is clean before merging into it.

workflow on that branch.** On 2026-08-18 I used it to confirm master was green after merging #385,
got `completed success`, and reported it. The jobs were `build` and `deploy`: it was the **Pages**

This repo has four workflows (`ci.yml`, `pages.yml`, `publish-mcp.yml`, `release.yml`), and Pages
runs on every push to master, so it very often wins the `--limit 1` race.

unless you ask for it. A green from the wrong workflow looks exactly like a green from the right
one.

## The tell

I pushed a follow-up commit to a branch I had pushed several times, and git said:

```
 * [new branch]        claude/audit-fixes-0-9-7 -> claude/audit-fixes-0-9-7
```

Not `6efbdb47..827ff8e1`. The remote branch had been **deleted when its PR merged**, and my push
recreated it from my local state, which was the pre-merge state plus one commit.

## Why that is dangerous rather than untidy

Two PRs had landed meanwhile (see [[stacked-prs-cascade-on-merge]] for how they both reached
master). My branch still held the six original commits, so `git diff origin/master` showed **2145
deletions**: opening a PR from there would have reverted the second one entirely.

1. **A broad `except` and a test double are a trap together.** Each is defensible alone. Together,
   any method the double is missing becomes an exercise of the error branch that looks like the
   success branch to a substring assertion.
2. **Assert the thing only the success path can produce.** The fix was `"quickstart_chunks/quickstart
   (22)" in detail` plus `"not counted in time" not in detail`. A row COUNT cannot be produced by
   the branch that failed to count.
3. **Mutation testing found it, and a passing test did not.** The mutation "make the count query
   always raise" was expected to turn the test red and did not, which is what exposed it. A guard
   you have not watched fail is not a guard; that rule caught this one.

not there.

## 🔑 The lessons

- **Capture RED against the commit the fix actually changes.** One test here was captured against an

**A third form, same root: a squash-merged branch looks unmerged forever.** Squashing rewrites the
content into one new commit, so the source branch's original commits are never ancestors of master
and `git log origin/master..HEAD` keeps listing them. "5 commits ahead of master" on such a branch
is not evidence of pending work.

Measured 2026-08-18: I merged master into `claude/enterprise-rag-dense-floor`, reported it as "worth
a second merge before it goes in", and only checked afterwards that its PR #334 had been **merged
three days earlier**, squashed as `6ce37b4c`. The real additions over master were 10 insertions
across 14 files, not the 4 commits the log showed. Ask the forge, not the commit graph:

**How to apply:** ancestry against `HEAD` is never evidence about master. Ask the question that
matters, at the START and again before merging, and read it as a supersession signal:

git log --oneline HEAD..master -- <the files you are about to touch>

Any output means someone changed those files ahead of you. `git merge-tree $(git merge-base HEAD
master) HEAD master | grep "changed in both"` confirms it in one more command. And when a commit is
"not an ancestor", the next command is `git branch -a --contains <sha>` INCLUDING master, not a
conclusion.

The push still landed on bypass, so this is a warning rather than a wall, but `master` now carries
a commit the repo's own ruleset rejects. That is worth knowing BEFORE choosing how to land work:
squash-merge satisfies both rules at once, which is probably why it was the recommended route in
the first place. The cost is real, though, and worth stating to the user rather than assuming:
squashing discards commit bodies AND collapses any `git merge` commits that deliberately preserve
another branch's history and authorship. When a branch is a consolidation of several branches,
that is the whole point of it, so ask which matters more instead of defaulting.

## The design decision (asked, not assumed)

`StoreRegistry` takes a fixed `allowed_tenants` and documents that the tenant set comes from
configuration and **never from traffic**. OIDC has no enumerable tenant set (tenants arrive inside
tokens), so wiring it in without an allowlist would have deleted that property silently.

**Why:** the cascade is invisible in the request. I intended to merge one PR into a feature branch
and instead merged two into master, one of them (`d5494708`) with its CI **red** — its failing jobs
were never re-run, because the branch it would have re-run on was merged in the same instant. The
tip stayed green only because the fixing commit landed one second later. A bisect that lands on
`d5494708` still fails today for reasons unrelated to whatever is being bisected.

**How to apply:**

- **Pre-merge CI matters**: PR #878 was merged before lazy-psycopg2 fix → master broke for CI envs. Avoid `--admin` merge if checks pending. Cherry-pick recovery worked but introduced extra PR (#882).

# Un PR "stacked" si mergia nella sua BASE, non in master

Su mem-bench il 2026-08-02: PR #62 aperto con base `fix/board-audit-findings-55` (per impilarlo su
#61). Mergiati entrambi a 7 secondi di distanza. Risultato:

```
$ gh pr view 62 --json state   -> MERGED
$ git merge-base --is-ancestor 556c377 origin/master   -> NO
```

🔑 **GitHub ri-punta un PR stacked su `master` SOLO quando la sua base viene CANCELLATA dopo il
merge.** Se la base esiste ancora al momento del merge, il PR si mergia **nella base** e il
contenuto non arriva mai a master. Lo stato resta `MERGED` in entrambi i casi, quindi
**non c'è nessun segnale rosso**: sembra fatto.

baseline.text:
**A third form, same root: a squash-merged branch looks unmerged forever.** Squashing rewrites the
content into one new commit, so the source branch's original commits are never ancestors of master
and `git log origin/master..HEAD` keeps listing them. "5 commits ahead of master" on such a branch
is not evidence of pending work.

Measured 2026-08-18: I merged master into `claude/enterprise-rag-dense-floor`, reported it as "worth
a second merge before it goes in", and only checked afterwards that its PR #334 had been **merged
three days earlier**, squashed as `6ce37b4c`. The real additions over master were 10 insertions
across 14 files, not the 4 commits the log showed. Ask the forge, not the commit graph:

**How to apply:** ancestry against `HEAD` is never evidence about master. Ask the question that
matters, at the START and again before merging, and read it as a supersession signal:

git log --oneline HEAD..master -- <the files you are about to touch>

Any output means someone changed those files ahead of you. `git merge-tree $(git merge-base HEAD
master) HEAD master | grep "changed in both"` confirms it in one more command. And when a commit is
"not an ancestor", the next command is `git branch -a --contains <sha>` INCLUDING master, not a
conclusion.

The push still landed on bypass, so this is a warning rather than a wall, but `master` now carries
a commit the repo's own ruleset rejects. That is worth knowing BEFORE choosing how to land work:
squash-merge satisfies both rules at once, which is probably why it was the recommended route in
the first place. The cost is real, though, and worth stating to the user rather than assuming:
squashing discards commit bodies AND collapses any `git merge` commits that deliberately preserve
another branch's history and authorship. When a branch is a consolidation of several branches,
that is the whole point of it, so ask which matters more instead of defaulting.

which discards the commit body. This repo's history carries substantial commit bodies (see

`master`. Pushing a local `git merge --no-ff` printed

```
remote: Bypassed rule violations for refs/heads/master:
remote: - This branch must not contain merge commits.
remote:   Found 1 violation:  f8e8f21...
```

   not wanted, retarget or cherry-pick first. The "merge into the feature branch, then merge the
   feature branch" plan does not survive a stack.

"not an ancestor", the next command is `git branch -a --contains <sha>` INCLUDING master, not a
conclusion.

- `conv_purity` predicted **0.55–0.65** → actual **0.503**, chance. `doc_purity` predicted

🔑 And the invariant guard I wrote to check the artifacts **over-fired**: `excised_doc_ids` are
CHUNK ids (`conv-26/D10:20`), and comparing at DOCUMENT granularity flagged every surviving sibling
chunk — 2295 phantom "leaks". Corrected to exact-id comparison it **PASSES 0/1200**. Same class the
ladder audit hit four times, this time in my own check: *audit the guard itself*.
[[feedback-audit-the-guard-itself-not-just-what-it-guards-2026-07-29]]

| code state | test on the consumer | test on the backfill path |
|---|---|---|
| both releases present | pass | pass |
| no `store_sparse_vectors` close | **FAIL** | pass |
| no backfill `closing()` | pass | pass |
| neither (original) | **FAIL** | **FAIL** |

🔑 **No mutation distinguishes the backfill's `closing()`.** Once the consumer closes the genexp,
the genexp's reference was the cursor's last one, so CPython finalises it there and then. The
wrapper is harmless defence-in-depth but it is **not** a second thing under test, and a docstring
claiming it is would be a guard that reads as protection and cannot fire —
[[feedback-a-guard-that-reads-as-protection-and-cannot-fire-2026-07-30]]. I wrote the matrix into
the test docstring rather than the claim.

## How to apply

🔑 The sharper version of the standing lesson: *a guard that reads as protection and cannot fire*
has a twin — **a guard that cannot PASS**. Both look like rigour in a document and neither tests
anything. Asking "what would make this fire?" catches the first; **"what would make this pass?"**
is the question I was not asking.

## What it cost, and what caught it

`bug-auditor` caught F3 (before publication) and would have caught C4; D1 I caught only because I
ran the check anyway. The direct cost was a verdict claiming a "textbook" control that was 96%
arithmetic, and a FALSIFIED verdict on a perfectly valid run. **Two of three were caught before
anything shipped — by the audit, not by me.**

`"registered"`, printed a success
line, and wrote to a file the client does not read, with six tests passing. It was found by running
the wizard path by hand ten minutes after a 129-passed run.

**Why:** in every case the defect lived in the interaction between a test and its platform or its
collaborator, not in anything visible on screen. Review cannot find these by construction, and
mutating the code under test does not either, because the mutation dies against an assertion that
was never running.

**How to apply**, three clauses, cheapest first:

1. **Before trusting a guard, break what it guards and watch it fail.** Two minutes. If it stays
   green the test is measuring the platform, not the code.
2. **Guard the fixture, not just the behaviour.** A derived count

**Why:** [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] covers guards that never fire because the assertion was
unsatisfiable or too narrow from the start. This is the adjacent failure: a guard that used to
fire, and quietly stops, because it depends on a string/event contract nobody versioned. The
guard-test in that memory (mutate and watch it go red) catches the first kind but not this one,
because the mutation target is the code under test, not the upstream tool the gate depends on.

🔑 **A guard over INDICES is not a guard over the property when the property is over NAMES.** One
duplicated project name left the index arithmetic perfectly disjoint and still reproduced the bug.
🔑 **Measure a slice against the sequence it is APPLIED to**, not against a constant and not against
an imaginary `indices(10_000)`. Both wrong denominators passed, then died on a bare `IndexError`.
🔑 **A hand-kept pair list beside an enumerable dict is ABSENT, not red**, when a fourth item
arrives. `itertools.combinations(sorted(sets), 2)`.
🔑 **Two comments cited tests that had never existed**, while new guards leaned on the facts those
comments claimed were pinned. Grep the test name before trusting "pinned by a test".
🔑 **Weakening an assertion and watching it still pass proves nothing** — a

**Why:** the credibility of a guard is a shared resource. Every false alarm spends it, and it is
spent silently, so the guard still looks installed long after it stopped being believed.

**How to apply:** when a guard contradicts something you have directly observed, treat that as a
bug report against the guard and open its source before dismissing it. Check specifically whether
the parse failure disables a detection further down, since an early return on unparsed input is the
usual shape. And when a guard's regex is the guard, keep its cases in the file and make them
runnable. Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]],
[[bug-reports-from-stale-checkouts]], [[missing-input-becomes-a-clean-null]].

- **After writing a guard, break the thing it guards and watch it go red.** Not the absence of the
  fix, the *wrong* fix. A regression test in this branch passed against `entries[-1]`, which
  coincidentally returns the right entry when there are exactly two; it only discriminated once it
  looped both orderings.
- **Capture RED against the commit the fix actually changes.** One test here was captured against an
  earlier commit where a *different* bug killed it first, so the assertion under test never ran. That
  looks identical to a correct capture unless you check which line the failure lands on.
- 🔑 **A guard on a helper is not a guard on the page.** The board's withholding test called
  `_fmt_figures_with_status` directly, so a new rendering surface routed around it and printed the

🔑 **Four times in one session the same shape appeared: a guard that reads as protection and cannot
fire.** Partial ingest faking a FAIL · absent data faking a FAIL · empty corpus faking a PASS · a
vacuous test. Assume the class.

---

🔑 **MY POSITION TEST WAS INSUFFICIENT, AND NAMEABLY SO.** It compared gold EARLY vs LATE *within*
long contexts (mean −0.102, 15/30 — passed). Both arms were long, so a defect degrading BOTH
equally cancels in the difference. **It varied POSITION while holding LENGTH constant, so it could
never detect a LENGTH effect** — it could catch "the tail is ignored", not "the whole thing is
degraded". The test that would have caught it: same gold, SHORT vs LONG context, comparing
*absolute* `null_odds`. Third vacuous-guard instance in this arc, and the subtlest: **controlling
for the wrong variable**. [[feedback-audit-the-guard-itself-not-just-what-it-guards-2026-07-29]]

because it is the reason the guard exists. The traffic it must let through gets tested by nobody, and
a guard that blocks legitimate work is removed by the person it blocks, which loses the coverage
entirely. This is the mirror image of [[guards-that-cannot-fail]]: that one is a gate that never
fires, this is a gate that fires on the ordinary case.

**How to apply:** when writing or auditing a gate, write the ALLOW table first and make it concrete.
For a git guard that means the idioms actually typed daily, not a paraphrase of them. The fix here
was one condition, and the verification that made it trustworthy was ten push forms checked at once,
including the two that must still be refused. The same probe caught that the pathspec guard nearby
gets this right: it parses the

**CORRECTED 2026-08-11.** I previously wrote here that a DB-less run is *much slower*, because each
unguarded connection burns the psycopg connect timeout. Measured, it is the opposite. With nothing
listening on 5432, `python -m pytest -q` finished in **313 s (5m12s)**, 3128 passed / 516 skipped /
1 xfailed. The DB tests do not hang: a fixture guard skips them with the reason `pgvector DB not
reachable (run 'docker compose up -d')`, 41 of them in `test_enterprise_integration.py` alone.

So the two shapes of a green run are:

- container up: ~705 s, ~3259 passed, ~26 skipped
- container down: ~313 s, 3128 passed, **516 skipped**

Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]], [[guards-placed-after-the-action]],
[[plan-constraints-need-per-path-verification]].

**How to apply:** `except urllib.error.URLError` does **NOT** cover all urllib transport
faults — always pair it with `http.client.HTTPException` + `ConnectionError`. Applies to
every stdlib-urllib client in the repo. 🔑 hundreds of handled `network err, retry` WARNINGs
next to a fatal crash of the *same family* = the except tuple is too narrow, not the network.

## Cross-cutting

A red unit is a claim, not a diagnosis — **read what the guard actually measured before
"fixing" the thing it accuses.** Both of these would have been "fixed" wrongly by forcing a
rebuild / raising a threshold, leaving the real defect (a guard with no diagnostic power) in
place. Corollary to [[feedback-verify-collector-terminal-table-2026-07-14]]: verify the
guard's *semantics*, not just that it is armed.

**Why:** reviewing a guard tends to check "does this correctly implement the rule?" rather than
"can the rule be satisfied without being true?" Those are different questions, and only the second
finds a laundering path. The per-task reviewers each saw one diff and judged it against its brief;
the audit asked an adversarial question the briefs never posed.

**How to apply:**

Writing a literal U+2028 into a Python test file via the editing tools is unreliable. On
2026-08-11, in `tests/test_fix.py`, the same pasted character survived in one test and was
silently turned into an ordinary space (U+0020) in two others written minutes later.

**Why it matters more than it sounds:** the affected tests were guards ABOUT line separators. With
the separator flattened to a space, one guard passed against the unfixed code and another failed
against the fixed code, that is, the results inverted. Nothing in the pytest output looked wrong;
only dumping the source's actual code points found it. This is [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] arriving
through the editor rather than through the assertion.

The lesson worth keeping is not about embedders: **I recorded a consequence I had inferred from
reading a guard, without running the case.** The guard was real and its reach was a third of what I
claimed. Related: [[audit-findings-need-reproducing]].

`scripts/session-mcp-close.sh` has a guard that stops it killing the ssh it is itself running,
whose command line necessarily contains the pattern it searches for. The tests had a fixture row
for exactly that process, the suite was green, and **deleting the guard kept it green**.

The reason is the interesting part. The fixture parented that ssh to `__SELF__` (the script's own
pid) but never put `__SELF__` itself in the process table. So the ownership walk failed at the
first hop and the process was excluded for **the wrong reason**: not "it is mine", but "its parent
is unknown". Every assertion still passed with the real guard removed. The repair was one fixture
line placing the script under the session client, which is where it really sits.

2. **5-fold time-based CV** (walk-forward, table in §4.2). Per-fold pass

3. **4 baselines**, all must lose:

My single most repeated defect on this project, across ~35 instances since 2026-08-06. The shape
is always the same: **I write the assertion that describes the behaviour I intend, not the one
that fails when the behaviour is gone.** Those feel identical while writing and are completely
different in effect. Reading the test never finds it. Only running a mutation does.

## The rule

**Delete or invert the behaviour a guard names, and watch it go red.** If it stays green, the
guard is decoration. One command. In reports, say WHICH mutations ran and what happened, never
"verified".

Three refinements that each cost me a round:

session landed 11 of my 12 commits; also closes/rebases PRs under you, and a stale base looks exactly like a regression.
- [Renaming a project forks its memory](renaming-a-project-forks-its-memory.md) — the store key is the PATH; the RE-call rename hid two memos for ten days while I worked the same bug from the other half.
- [Guards placed after the action](guards-placed-after-the-action.md) — I wrote the token file THEN checked it was ignored, with the right invariant in the comment above the wrong code; a mutation test proves a guard fires, not that it fires in time.
- [Blockers outlive their cause](blockers-outlive-their-cause.md) — a spec sat at "blocked on VPS2" for 13 days after VPS2 recovered; pair a block with the condition that clears it, and date one against the world before

- **A pre-filter may be sloppy; a decision may not.** The `case` in `settings.json` that decides
  whether to *invoke* a guard can over-match harmlessly, because the script then decides. The script
  itself cannot.
- **One residual false positive is known and left in place.** Backticks inside single quotes are not
  command substitution to a shell, but the parser treats them as such. It over-detects, which is the
  safe direction for a guard, and it is documented rather than silently accepted.

Related: [[test-a-guards-allow-path]] is the same session's other half, a guard refusing correct
work. [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] is the opposite failure. [[a-detector-with-no-sink]] completes the
set: fires and is discarded, fires wrongly, never fires.

## Audit (CCA DEEP, 11 auditors, 40 raw → 7 P1)
Two of MY published claims were wrong and are corrected by dated note, not silent edit: a headline
naming a contrast that never ran, and "decreases" that were non-increases. Also fixed: a v1 rebuild
would have advertised v2 semantics **with the same digest**; the non-empty-table guard cited a
`--table` flag that did not exist; `assert_manifest_digest` was never called though the spec
advertised five invariants; and a test guarding *the label must never be a lie* passed vacuously
(proven by mutation). Orchestration lessons →
[[feedback-verify-at-the-same-scope-the-gate-uses-2026-07-29]].

I guarded one direction only.** The docstring names a labeller "that
can only ever answer false positive". Nothing anywhere proved the labellers could answer TRUE on
real data. That is the direction producing the comfortable number, and it was the unguarded one.
A control needs both a case that must pass and a case that must fail.

**How to apply:**

- A control must reach the value by a DIFFERENT path than the code under test. Re-parse the row,
  re-embed the text, recompute from the raw source. If the control's two inputs are the same
  object, the comparison is an identity, not a test.
- Say out loud what input would make the guard fire. If the answer is "an implementation that
  ignores its arguments", it is decoration.
- Mutate the code to prove the guard can fail, per

**Why:** mutation testing proves a guard *can* fail, and a green suite proves *some* bytes pass.
Neither says the bytes tested are the bytes being pushed. Those diverge whenever a fix is staged,
in flight, or mid-mutation, which on a long session is most of the time.

**How to apply:** before pushing, verify the artifact rather than the tree. `git archive <sha>` to a
scratchpad and run there, or at minimum `git status --short` plus `git diff HEAD --stat` and confirm
both are empty before quoting a suite result as evidence for a commit. When dispatching a reviewer,
tell it to audit the commit, not the checkout. Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]],
[[subagents-commit-to-wrong-worktree]].

🔑 The closed form is `if meta.get("providers_source") != "session": refuse` — require the
known-good value. It rejects nothing the producer emits and everything it does not.

🔑 **A test that hand-crafts an input the producer cannot produce is not a test of the guard.**
That is how #3 shipped green.

↔ Same family as [[feedback-a-guard-that-reads-as-protection-and-cannot-fire-2026-07-30]] and
[[feedback-check-the-deciding-cell-has-power-2026-08-06]]. What is new here is the *repair*
inheriting the defect, and that only an audit by other agents caught it.

⚠️ **And I ticked the PR checklist wrongly.** I wrote "No dependency version changed. ragas is added
as an optional extra only", which is exactly the case the template's `uv lock` box exists for.
Adding an extra IS a dependency change. Reading the checkbox as a formality rather than a question
is how a wrong claim gets committed in writing.

Related: [[verify-the-commit-not-the-worktree]], [[guards-that-cannot-fail]].

it is decoration.
- Mutate the code to prove the guard can fail, per
  [[feedback-mutate-the-code-to-prove-a-test-can-fail-2026-08-01]]. Reading I4 satisfied me; running
  the mutation took two minutes and refuted it.
- Pair every "can return zero" control with a "can return one" control.

Same session, same module, an adjacent instance: I3 asserted `cos(q, q) == 1`, an algebraic identity
for every non-zero vector, with the only failing input (the zero vector) already rejected by I5 two
lines earlier. So two of seven invariants could not fire, in a module whose docstring argues twice
that a guard which cannot fire is decoration, and which had already rewritten I1 for exactly that
reason. **Knowing the rule is not applying it.**

Prior:

1. **A broad `except` and a test double are a trap together.** Each is defensible alone. Together,
   any method the double is missing becomes an exercise of the error branch that looks like the
   success branch to a substring assertion.
2. **Assert the thing only the success path can produce.** The fix was `"quickstart_chunks/quickstart
   (22)" in detail` plus `"not counted in time" not in detail`. A row COUNT cannot be produced by
   the branch that failed to count.
3. **Mutation testing found it, and a passing test did not.** The mutation "make the count query
   always raise" was expected to turn the test red and did not, which is what exposed it. A guard
   you have not watched fail is not a guard; that rule caught this one.

Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]], the same session's other lesson, that the mutation LIST is
the weak link once the technique is sound. Both failures were about the frame around the evidence,
not the evidence. [[a-detector-with-no-sink]] is the mirror image, where a docstring CLAIMED a
mechanism that did not exist and I nearly believed it; here I denied one that did. Both are fixed by
reading the code rather than the surrounding signal.

red and names the instrument. Each asserts the
task's actual discriminator, not a proxy: numeric order must differ from lexicographic
(`ts-natural-order`), at least one hidden file (`ts-glob-hidden`), at least one file at all
(`ts-manifest-rel`), and BOTH a cross-supplier id reuse and a redelivery (`fa-dedup-key`, whose
two wrong answers are disarmed by different thinnings). `tests/test_oracle_wellformedness.py`
pins it: 5 degradations plus 4 assertions that the committed oracles stay clean. Mutation-checked
(guard returns None -> all 5 red). Suite went 857 to 866 passed, 13 skipped.

The three unguarded ones are unguarded on purpose: `ts-golden-regen` and `ts-mig-name` raise on a
thinned oracle, and `xs-widen-manifest` fails honestly, so all three already fail closed.

⚠️ **Pre-registering it did not protect me.** I had already recorded [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] as
my recurring failure mode, and writing the prediction down in advance gave the same mistake a
ceremonial stamp. The protocol catches fitting a story to a number; it does not catch registering a
quantity whose value is determined before any data exists.

**How to apply.** Before committing a registration, ask of each row: *what state of the world would
make this come out differently?* If the answer is "none", it is a **guard**, which is worth keeping
and worth testing, but it is not a result and must not be scored. Two specific smells:

**Prefer impossible over detectable.** A static guard proving every DB test carried `@requires_db`
was wrong three times, each caught by an auditor: it hid 161 of 363 tests behind wrapper fixtures,
then 17 more, then misclassified 227 locals, always green while the property went unchecked over
a growing share of the suite, because I derived truth from a hand-written list and kept widening
it. Making `make_store` call `pytest.skip()` deleted 574 lines of inference, is exact rather than
approximate, and protects the tests whose author forgot the mark, the entire population at risk.
Ask early: can I make this impossible instead of detectable?

- **Exercise the DETECTION path, not the green path** — construct the state that should trip it.
- **Never let an empty denominator, an empty input, or a missing file produce a number.** Raise, or
  return `None` and make the renderer print `n/a`. `0.0` and "no data" must not be the same output.
- **A guard that cannot PASS gets deleted, not obeyed.** mem-bench's `verify.yml` fired on every PR
  while its scope gate demanded a diff of exactly one file under `submissions/` — so it failed every
  maintenance PR, including the one that added it. An unsatisfiable gate is a guard with a countdown
  on it.
- **When you build a guard, replay the motivating defect INSIDE it** — see
  [[feedback-an-exclusion-can-blind-a-guard-to-its-own-motivating-defect-2026-07-29]].

**I nearly published unverified numbers.** The baseline-signature figures I first wrote (120/550,
220/220) came from an earlier pass. Re-deriving them from `RAG.json` returned **all zeros**, because
I had the file's structure wrong: it is not a flat list but 842 `tasks` × 10 `models` = 8420
`evaluations`, with metrics nested under `annotations.*.composite.value`. The original figures had
also silently folded in `target`, the **human reference, which is not a system**.

🔑 **Re-derive a number before putting it in public, even one you produced yourself.** The
conclusion survived; the scope did not, and the scope was what the sentence claimed.
↔ same family as *a sweep is only as wide as its key* in `CLAUDE-lessons.md`.

⚠️ Note the asymmetry that makes this dangerous: a cannot-fail guard produces a **false green**,
and a cannot-pass guard produces a **false red** that discards good work. I produced one of each in
the same session.

Related: [[feedback-a-guard-that-reads-as-protection-and-cannot-fire-2026-07-30]] (the twin) ·
[[feedback-a-guard-must-hold-on-its-own-output-2026-08-05]] ·
[[project-recall-mtrag-retrieval-coverage-bottleneck-2026-08-06]] (where all three occurred)

Un guard non è finito quando i suoi controlli passano. È finito quando la cosa che **restituisce**
soddisfa ancora quei controlli.

🔑 The sharper version of the standing lesson: *a guard that reads as protection and cannot fire*
has a twin — **a guard that cannot PASS**. Both look like rigour in a document and neither tests
anything. Asking "what would make this fire?" catches the first; **"what would make this pass?"**
is the question I was not asking.

## What it cost, and what caught it

`bug-auditor` caught F3 (before publication) and would have caught C4; D1 I caught only because I
ran the check anyway. The direct cost was a verdict claiming a "textbook" control that was 96%
arithmetic, and a FALSIFIED verdict on a perfectly valid run. **Two of three were caught before
anything shipped — by the audit, not by me.**

## What it cost, and what caught it

ran the check anyway. The direct cost was a verdict claiming a "textbook" control that was 96%

**Why:** [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] covers guards that never fire because the assertion was
unsatisfiable or too narrow from the start. This is the adjacent failure: a guard that used to
fire, and quietly stops, because it depends on a string/event contract nobody versioned. The
guard-test in that memory (mutate and watch it go red) catches the first kind but not this one,
because the mutation target is the code under test, not the upstream tool the gate depends on.

**Why:** the credibility of a guard is a shared resource. Every false alarm spends it, and it is
spent silently, so the guard still looks installed long after it stopped being believed.

**How to apply:** when a guard contradicts something you have directly observed, treat that as a
bug report against the guard and open its source before dismissing it. Check specifically whether
the parse failure disables a detection further down, since an early return on unparsed input is the
usual shape. And when a guard's regex is the guard, keep its cases in the file and make them
runnable. Related: [[guards-that-cannot-fail]],
[[bug-reports-from-stale-checkouts]], [[missing-input-becomes-a-clean-null]].

and a cannot-pass guard produces a **false red** that discards good work. I produced one of each in
the same session.

🔑 The sharper version of the standing lesson: *a guard that reads as protection and cannot fire*
has a twin — **a guard that cannot PASS**. Both look like rigour in a document and neither tests
anything. Asking "what would make this fire?" catches the first; **"what would make this pass?"**
is the question I was not asking.

## What it cost, and what caught it

`bug-auditor` caught F3 (before publication) and would have caught C4; D1 I caught only because I
ran the check anyway. The direct cost was a verdict claiming a "textbook" control that was 96%
arithmetic, and a FALSIFIED verdict on a perfectly valid run. **Two of three were caught before
anything shipped — by the audit, not by me.**

Un guard non è finito quando i suoi controlli passano. È finito quando la cosa che **restituisce**
soddisfa ancora quei controlli.

🔑 **Four times in one session the same shape appeared: a guard that reads as protection and cannot
fire.** Partial ingest faking a FAIL · absent data faking a FAIL · empty corpus faking a PASS · a
vacuous test. Assume the class.

---

**Why:** [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] covers guards that never fire because the assertion was
unsatisfiable or too narrow from the start. This is the adjacent failure: a guard that used to
fire, and quietly stops, because it depends on a string/event contract nobody versioned. The
guard-test in that memory (mutate and watch it go red) catches the first kind but not this one,
because the mutation target is the code under test, not the upstream tool the gate depends on.
