# Write-time relay and project scoping, PR 538, 2026-08-28

**What it changes.** The `PreToolUse` write-time hook was a process per tool call: import, connect,
one query, exit. PR 538 (`codex/write-time-relay-audit-fix`, commit `3faae6b4`, open) moves the
PostgreSQL connection into a **detached helper owned by the Claude session**, reached over loopback
TCP. Loopback rather than a UNIX socket so one implementation covers Windows. A random port is not
authentication, so every request carries a token from a 0600 state file keyed by
`sha256(session_id)[:32]`, never by the session id itself.

Two behaviour changes matter more than the latency:

⛔ **So a disagreement between the store and an index is not evidence of a broken store.** It is
equally likely to be a write in flight. Re-check before repairing, or you will "fix" an index that
was about to be correct and create a real conflict.

🔑 **Two habits that make this safe:**

- **Assert that an edit changed something.** `assert new != old` after every `str.replace` on a
  shared file. A no-op that reports success is worse than a crash.
- **Assert coverage, not counts.** Every memo reachable from exactly one sub-index is a property
  that stays true under concurrent writes. A number does not, and this store's stated count has
  now been wrong five times while coverage has never once broken.

**Why it works, and it is not subtle.** A draft contains the literal identifiers the memo's fix
line contains. One `ts-lf-rewrite` session wrote `version_file.write_text(content,
encoding="utf-8")`; the memo says `path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`. That is
a lexical match no amount of prose rewriting could manufacture, and it exists only in the artifact,
never in the goal. "You cannot look up a hazard you do not know exists" is true of the goal and
FALSE of the draft: the draft already contains the operation that will fail.

3. **In Python, rewrite per STRING TOKEN, not per line.** Inserting double quotes corrupts a
   double-quoted literal, and
   `pytest.importorskip("openai", reason="...pip install recall[bench]")` holds two literals on one
   line, a first-quote/last-quote swap breaks the wrong one. `tokenize` makes the delimiter
   decision for the string that actually contains the text.

- Prefer the Edit tool for file changes; it does not do this.
- If scripting an edit in Python, pass `newline="\n"`:
  `path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`.
- To diagnose: `git ls-files --eol <file>` shows index vs working-tree endings directly.
- To confirm a diff is line-endings-only, hash both sides normalised rather than trusting
  `git diff --ignore-all-space`, which also hides real whitespace changes:
  `git show HEAD:f | tr -d '\r' | sha256sum` against `tr -d '\r' < f | sha256sum`.
- To fix once content is confirmed identical: `git checkout -- <files>`. Do NOT commit it; the
  commit would record no content change.

Related: [[ruff-blocked-locally]] for the other local tooling gotcha in this repo.

This repo's `.gitattributes` sets `* text=auto eol=lf`, so the working tree is meant to be LF
even on Windows. `Path.write_text(...)` in Python's default text mode translates `\n` to `\r\n`
on Windows, so any file edited that way comes back as CRLF and git reports it modified forever,
with `warning: CRLF will be replaced by LF` on every add.

Observed 2026-08-07: after a session of scripted edits, `git status` showed `recall/retriever.py`
and `recall/store.py` as modified with **zero content difference**. `git ls-files --eol` showed
`i/lf w/crlf`, i.e. index LF, working tree CRLF.

**How to apply:**

⚠️ Same session, a second way a "successful" write leaves the wrong state, unrelated to concurrency.
My mutation harness restored each file with `path.write_text(original)` and verified the restore by
comparing a hash of `read_text`. It passed. `git status` still showed the file **modified**: on
Windows `write_text` had converted the whole file **LF → CRLF**, and `read_text` universalises
newlines on read, so the hash could not see what the write had done. Had I committed, the diff would
have been every line of `recall/lineage.py`.
🔑 **A hash taken through a normalising read cannot verify a write.** Verify a restore with
`git diff --stat` (or `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` to separate content from endings), not with a
checksum you computed yourself. Same family as *diff the file

Build awkward characters with `chr(0xDCFF)`, or bind them to a named constant in the target file
(`BOM = b"\xef\xbb\xbf"`), rather than writing the escape inline. Print `ascii(value)` at the top
of a probe so the input is visible in the output. Tests and source written through the editor are
fine; it is only the shell transport that mangles.

🔁 **2026-08-15: violated three times in one session, and the second and third came AFTER I had
named this rule out loud.** `\\t` and `\\r` became a literal tab and CR inside a test file;
backticks in a `python -c` became command substitution; `\xef\xbb\xbf` and `\n` became a decoded
BOM and a real line break, leaving a file that would not parse. Each cost a correction round.

🔇 **2026-08-15, the failure mode that does not announce itself: a SILENT no-op.** A fourth
violation in the same session, and the worst-behaved. I sent a heredoc whose search string
contained `\n` inside a triple-quoted Python string, intending to replace a function definition.
The transport altered the string, `str.replace` found no match, **returned the original
unchanged**, and the script printed its success message. Three later edits in the same script DID
apply, so the file was left half-edited and syntactically broken in a way that only surfaced at
the next run.

`str.replace` and `re.sub` do not raise on a miss. Every earlier instance of this rule at least
produced a wrong VALUE I could see; this one produced no output at all.

refuses to start, because a server silently serving a smaller surface than configured is
indistinguishable from an agent choosing not to call the missing tool.

recall ships an MCP server (`recall_mcp`, 10 tools) and `docs/USING_WITH_CLAUDE.md` documents
exactly how to install it. The project did not use it on itself. It does now:

Measured 2026-08-16, by probing every server directly over MCP streamable HTTP
rather than by opinion:

- **All five internal servers are live and reachable** on the tailnet.
  `qwen-mcp` is `qwen-agent 1.27.0` with **33 tools**.
- `code_search`, `db_query_ro` and `rg_search_live` all returned correct results
  **first try, with correct arguments**. The documented 17.1% error rate is
  caller error, confirmed rather than assumed.
- **`.mcp.json` existed in 4 of 41 checkouts.** recall 3 of 21, sentiment-agent
  **1 of 20**. So 37 of 41 sessions began with no MCP servers at all.

# What this records

Authenticated MCP mutations now persist their completed response in the PostgreSQL audit table
before attempting Redis response caching. A retry whose Redis marker exists but whose Redis result
is missing checks the tenant scoped PostgreSQL receipt and replays it. If both stores lack the
response, the server returns `reconciliation_required` and does not execute the mutation again.

The receipt identity is a SHA 256 derived event ID, so the client idempotency key is not written to
the audit table. Keep the PostgreSQL receipt lookup and the Redis cache write in this order when
changing mutation response handling.

## 5. §2b deadman checks (local scheduled tasks)
`gate-check-1895-2026-07-30`, `gate-check-1897-2026-07-30`, `gate-check-1896-2026-08-06` — each runs the gate-check + posts the verdict (run when the app is open / next launch).

**Why:** CLAUDE.md §2b makes every gate carry a scheduled check as its deadman, but there is no
inverse rule. An orphaned deadman is worse than a missing one: it arrives with confident,
self-contained instructions and no knowledge that the lane died, so the default behaviour is to
re-run a closed experiment and post numbers that invite a reopen. The scheduled task's own
framing is stale data, not authority — [[feedback-verify-collector-terminal-table-2026-07-14]]
is the same failure shape one layer down.

🔑 **A local suite proves the code runs in MY environment, not that it runs.** The two failure modes
are symmetric and both invisible from here: a package I happen to have, and a binary I happen to
have. A test that calls `resolve_claude_executable()` is testing my laptop.

Three rules that follow:

1. **A new import needs a declaration, not just an install.** `import scipy` in shipped code is a
   dependency even when the module is a benchmark helper.
2. **A test that needs an external binary must skip without it**, not fail. `pytest.importorskip`
   and a `shutil.which` guard are the whole fix.
3. **Run what CI runs before pushing**, which here is more than pytest: `python -m mypy`,
   `uv lock --check`, and `pip-audit`. Ruff plus pytest is two of five gates.

query.query: is it enough for a guard to refuse known-bad values

baseline_items.text:
**Refusing known-BAD values is a negative check. It closes only the failure modes you thought of,
and everything the producer never emits — or that predates the field — walks straight through.**

Measured, RE-call `fix/beam-artifact-rejudgeable`, 2026-08-07. I wrote `embed_parity.py` to stop a
GPU-vs-CPU comparison silently running CPU-vs-CPU. Three guards in it could not fire:

🔑 The closed form is `if meta.get("providers_source") != "session": refuse` — require the
known-good value. It rejects nothing the producer emits and everything it does not.

🔑 **A test that hand-crafts an input the producer cannot produce is not a test of the guard.**
That is how #3 shipped green.

↔ Same family as [[feedback-a-guard-that-reads-as-protection-and-cannot-fire-2026-07-30]] and
[[feedback-check-the-deciding-cell-has-power-2026-08-06]]. What is new here is the *repair*
inheriting the defect, and that only an audit by other agents caught it.

- **A pre-filter may be sloppy; a decision may not.** The `case` in `settings.json` that decides
  whether to *invoke* a guard can over-match harmlessly, because the script then decides. The script
  itself cannot.
- **One residual false positive is known and left in place.** Backticks inside single quotes are not
  command substitution to a shell, but the parser treats them as such. It over-detects, which is the
  safe direction for a guard, and it is documented rather than silently accepted.

Related: [[test-a-guards-allow-path]] is the same session's other half, a guard refusing correct
work. [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] is the opposite failure. [[a-detector-with-no-sink]] completes the
set: fires and is discarded, fires wrongly, never fires.

- **Enumerate mutants from the SOURCE, top to bottom, not from the guards you remember.** I once
  mutated 25 guards, reached 24/25 and called it verified; an auditor enumerated from the file,
  ran 51, and 26 survived, including the identity cross-check the whole design existed for
  (it compared one of its four columns) and a type loop whose deletion makes a bad row *served as
  a hit* rather than refused.
- **A guard with a long comment defending it is a positive signal it is untested.** The author
  explained it instead of pinning it. `rollback()`, a `close()` on the refusal path, and an mkdir
  block were each argued for at length and pinned by nothing.
- **A guard with N conjoined terms needs N tests, one per term.** A single test can only ever see
  one term, because it varies one

⚠️ Note the asymmetry that makes this dangerous: a cannot-fail guard produces a **false green**,
and a cannot-pass guard produces a **false red** that discards good work. I produced one of each in
the same session.

query.query: does a clean git status mean I am on the tip of the branch

baseline_items.text:
## Why the usual checks did not catch it
- `git status --short` was **clean** — and clean says nothing about *which commit* you are on.
- The empirical test was real, reproducible, and executed the actual function. Running the code is
  normally the strongest evidence available; here it faithfully measured **the wrong tree**.
- Three sibling clones exist (`~/Documents/RE-call`, `re-call`, `recall`) on different branches.
  Picking one by name and finding a git repo is not picking the right one.

🔑 **Evidence quality does not survive a wrong substrate.** Verifying harder (running vs reading)
made the false finding *more* convincing, not less.

items.text:
- ⚠️ "Is this string already on master?" does NOT prove supersession either. It confirms that *almost* everything landed and that you have not yet found the residue.
- 🔑 For a **squash-merged** branch, `git log master..branch` lies — every commit looks unmerged.
- 🔑 The `ddd` ruleset was removed by the user, so `git push --delete` works.
- Record the SHAs before deleting: a deleted branch tip stays recoverable while the reflog holds it.

Related: [[feedback-concurrent-sessions-race-the-same-clone-2026-07-24]] — `git merge-tree` CLEAN does not mean no collision either.

**Why this bit me:** I ran `git checkout master 2>&1 | tail -2 && git merge --squash <branch>`. The
pipe made `&&` read `tail`'s exit status, not the failed checkout's, so the squash merge ran against
the *feature branch* that happened to be checked out, leaving 13 staged additions and two
conflicted files in the user's working tree. `git reset --hard HEAD` restored it because nothing was
committed and the tree had been clean.

**How to apply:** Check `git worktree list` before assuming any branch can be checked out. Never
pipe a command whose exit status gates a `&&` chain; capture the status explicitly instead. And
check the target worktree is clean before merging into it.

## Why the usual checks did not catch it
- `git status --short` was **clean** — and clean says nothing about *which commit* you are on.
- The empirical test was real, reproducible, and executed the actual function. Running the code is
  normally the strongest evidence available; here it faithfully measured **the wrong tree**.
- Three sibling clones exist (`~/Documents/RE-call`, `re-call`, `recall`) on different branches.
  Picking one by name and finding a git repo is not picking the right one.

🔑 **Evidence quality does not survive a wrong substrate.** Verifying harder (running vs reading)
made the false finding *more* convincing, not less.

**How the five were cleaned, and why it was lossless.** Each differed from an already-rewritten
clean target by **exactly one file**, the audit, because the force-push had rewritten the same work
under new hashes. So the fix was not a rebase at all: `reset --hard` to the rewritten remote for
the two whose worktrees were clean, `git branch -f` for the three checked out nowhere. Verify the
same way before trusting any such shortcut, since commit counts look alarming after a rewrite and
mean nothing:

```bash
git diff --name-only <local-branch> <clean-target>
```

One file listed means same work, safe. Anything else means real divergence, rebase properly.

## How to apply — before using code to judge any claim
1. `git rev-parse HEAD` vs `git rev-parse origin/@{u}` (after `git fetch`) — or just
   `git status -sb`, whose `[behind N]` is the part that matters. `--short` alone HIDES it.
2. When several clones of one repo exist, confirm the remote AND the branch AND the distance from
   the tip before reading a line.

   **your inputs** first. These docs are written at implementation time by the person who wrote the

baseline_items.text: Before deploying any sudoers lockdown that replaces wildcard `NOPASSWD: ALL` with a Cmnd_Alias allowlist, **verify whether the target user has a password set**. Without one, sudo for any non-allowlisted command silently fails with "a terminal is required to read the password" — the operator is locked out of every ad-hoc admin operation, and even console root login becomes the only recovery path.

**How to apply:**
- Step 0 (always): `sudo passwd -S <user>` (or `sudo grep <user>: /etc/shadow | cut -d: -f2`) — if it shows `L` / `*` / empty hash, no password is set.
- If no password: ask the operator before deploy, *"do you want me to set a password first (so non-allowlist commands prompt + work) or accept that the allowlist is a hard wall?"*. Do not assume.
- Even when a password exists, double-check the operator can recover via console — every Cmnd_Alias deploy needs a documented break-glass path that's been tested.
- Keep the pre-deploy file backup at a path the new sudoers still permits to read (so post-deploy rollback to the prior policy is possible from the same shell). The 2026-05-05 deploy left the backup at `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment.bak.<TS>` — DENIED to read by the new

**Why:** 2026-05-05 redteam fix session. Saw `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment: sentiment ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL` and assumed "NOPASSWD" implied "no password set". Deployed Cmnd_Alias lockdown. User immediately hit `[sudo] password for sentiment:` prompts when running outside the allowlist (e.g., `tee /etc/contabo/credentials.env`, `docker compose up -d` for a config refresh). The password actually *was* set, but the user couldn't remember it — equivalent to no fallback. Recovery options collapsed to (a) Contabo VNC console root login (operator did not have access at that moment) or (b) a destructive snapshot revert (the 2026-05-05 attempt got 400/404 from the Contabo API depending on body shape — `{}` body returns 404 'Cannot POST', empty body returns 400 'body cannot be empty'). baseline.text: Before deploying any sudoers lockdown that replaces wildcard `NOPASSWD: ALL` with a Cmnd_Alias allowlist, **verify whether the target user has a password set**. Without one, sudo for any non-allowlisted command silently fails with "a terminal is required to read the password" — the operator is locked out of every ad-hoc admin operation, and even console root login becomes the only recovery path.

**How to apply:**
- Step 0 (always): `sudo passwd -S <user>` (or `sudo grep <user>: /etc/shadow | cut -d: -f2`) — if it shows `L` / `*` / empty hash, no password is set.
- If no password: ask the operator before deploy, *"do you want me to set a password first (so non-allowlist commands prompt + work) or accept that the allowlist is a hard wall?"*. Do not assume.
- Even when a password exists, double-check the operator can recover via console — every Cmnd_Alias deploy needs a documented break-glass path that's been tested.
- Keep the pre-deploy file backup at a path the new sudoers still permits to read (so post-deploy rollback to the prior policy is possible from the same shell). The 2026-05-05 deploy left the backup at `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment.bak.<TS>` — DENIED to read by the new

**Why:** 2026-05-05 redteam fix session. Saw `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment: sentiment ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL` and assumed "NOPASSWD" implied "no password set". Deployed Cmnd_Alias lockdown. User immediately hit `[sudo] password for sentiment:` prompts when running outside the allowlist (e.g., `tee /etc/contabo/credentials.env`, `docker compose up -d` for a config refresh). The password actually *was* set, but the user couldn't remember it — equivalent to no fallback. Recovery options collapsed to (a) Contabo VNC console root login (operator did not have access at that moment) or (b) a destructive snapshot revert (the 2026-05-05 attempt got 400/404 from the Contabo API depending on body shape — `{}` body returns 404 'Cannot POST', empty body returns 400 'body cannot be empty'). query.query: why can gate 1774 never turn green

items.text:
**Why:** this is a specific instance of the standing rule that **a gate that cannot go green tells
you only about itself**. A gate failing on infrastructure drift is worse than one failing on a
finding, because the red is attributed to the plumbing and the missing coverage is never noticed.
It also rhymes with **CI GREEN ≠ CHECKED** — here it was CI RED ≠ CHECKED, same blind spot.

⇒ **3 fills is a conservative LOWER BOUND** against a measured 87k–4.8M share queue at the touch —
it is a statement about our simulator's blindness to cancels, **not** a market fact that resting at
the touch does not fill. Real books drain by cancellation too. The hypothesis is **still untested**.

## Why it was not re-dated

This is the **2nd phantom-gate diagnosis on this same gate** (the 1st was 07-19, comment
`5015109734`). Both times the collector was alive and the gate still could not reach its bar.
Extending the date a third time without building (a) cancel attribution and (b) the markout writer
just re-runs the phantom. **A gate that cannot turn green only speaks about itself.**

### Gate #1774 EXTENDED 2026-08-15 → **2026-09-15**
The original window collected zero usable entries. Scheduled check armed
(`under-decay-gate-1774-check-2026-09-15`). If ~0 BUYs persist after two months of a *working* entry
window, that is close to a falsification of the edge — say so rather than extending a third time.

**2026-08-27, three times.** Every time CI went red on something a local run would have caught. The
first two were gates run *before* the change; the third was a gate my own filter never selected.

1. **mypy on PR #532.** I ran ruff and pytest after editing `sdk_exec.py` and did not re-run mypy,
   which had been green earlier. The new parameter was `StdioRecallSpec | None` where the callee
   wanted `StdioRecallSpec`.
2. **The citation gates after merging `recall_agent`.** My insertion in `recall/store.py` shifted
   every line below it by 26, invalidating four `path:line` citations in the docs. The gates had
   been green before the insertion.

**Why this keeps happening:** a green gate produces a feeling of coverage that outlives the state
it described, and nothing in the terminal distinguishes "green, and nothing has changed since" from
"green, four edits ago". It is exactly the staleness failure this project documents everywhere
else, applied to my own working memory instead of to a note.

**How to apply:**

- **The last thing before staging is the full gate set, in one command, from this worktree's root.**
  Not the subset that seems related: the mypy failure was in a file whose change looked purely
  additive, and the citation failure was in documents I never opened.

🔑 **The part worth keeping: 18 of the 24 were wrong and GREEN.** The anchor checker only fails when
the cited line's anchor falls outside its window, and a shift of a few lines stays inside it. So a
passing citation gate is evidence that a pointer is close, not that it is right, which is the same
shape as the note in `CLAUDE.md` about a green `git merge` not proving a server still serves.

Two rules this leaves standing: `docs/preregistrations/` and `docs/archive/` are frozen and were not
touched (the standing instruction forbids editing a number in a committed pre-registration, and a
gate must never force that edit), and a citation is better written against a SYMBOL than a line
where a symbol will do.

🔑 **A gate that cannot go green reports nothing about the tree — it only reports itself.** Same
family as the phantom-gate class and "`is-active` is not evidence a service works": #3 and #4 each
made the job *look* like it was checking something. Nobody had ever seen it pass, which should have
been the tell far earlier than it was.

## The verification mistake worth not repeating

— I called an archive missing after searching three drives; it was at `f83a330^`, and my filename filter could never have matched it.
- [External state in generated assets](external-state-in-generated-assets.md) — fetch it so a rebuild shows drift (caught Glama AAA→AAB); prose has no rebuild, and sample before believing one fetch.
- [Fixes leak outside the file you edited](fixes-leak-outside-the-file-you-edited.md) — 20 of 22 review findings were in my own fixes; test the artifact a reader opens, not the return value.
- [Green PR checks can predate a new CI job](green-pr-checks-can-predate-a-new-ci-job.md) — 8/8 SUCCESS and CLEAN described the jobs that existed at last build; a job master added afterwards never ran, and two green PRs turned master red on merge. **Compare check COUNTS, not

## Why it is not evidence in this benchmark's sense

The replacement counts in-flight CHUNKS, which rise whether an embedding came from the API or from
the cache, and tenants promoted, which is what the launch gate actually demands. Measured at the
time: 2,078 chunks/min on a cache-served rebuild that the old metric called stalled.

**How to apply:**

1. **Before choosing a progress metric, ask what would zero it.** If the answer is "an optimisation
   working", pick something else.
2. **Measure the artefact the job produces**, not a resource it consumes on the way: chunks written,
   records appended, conditions promoted — not cache rows, not CPU, not bytes read.
3. **A false stall is not harmless.** It trains the reader to ignore the watcher, which is worse
   than no watcher, and the real stall arrives later looking identical.

default `chunks`, which the quickstart creates (the global migrations are recorded against it and

to walk exactly that path.

## Meta-finding

**Isolation premium is conditional on signal-quality threshold.**

- **Above threshold (high-conviction signals): isolated > clustered.**
  Mechanism: the first big move after quiet captures maximum private information; subsequent moves leak / are partially priced.
- **Below threshold (low-conviction signals): clustered > isolated.**
  Mechanism: small/routine signals carry no info alone; they become informative only when many align (cluster = consensus). Classical Cohen-Malloy-Pomorski 2012.

## Reusable test template

For ANY new shadow candidate, run a 3-quadrant test:

```
                 isolated    clustered
high-conviction   ?          ?
low-conviction    ?          ?
```

If only clustered low-conviction has edge → classical theory.
If only isolated high-conviction has edge → our deployed pattern.

## 1. `nproc` honours `OMP_NUM_THREADS`

GNU coreutils `nproc` returns `min(OMP_NUM_THREADS, available)`. A script that exports
`OMP_NUM_THREADS=2` and then counts cores with `nproc` reads **2 on a twelve-core machine**. Measured:
`OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 nproc` → `2`; `nproc --all` → `12` (the `--all` path does not consult it).

That killed a launch outright: one fix set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to make a false comment true, another
counted cores to fail closed, and **three review rounds missed the interaction** because each read
the two hunks separately and nothing had run the script end to end.

## Maker rebates (maker-rebates)
- `fee_equivalent = C · feeRate · p · (1 − p)`  (C = shares filled, p = fill price, feeRate = category taker rate)
- `rebate = (your_fee_equivalent / total_fee_equivalent) · rebate_pool`
- Crypto: taker `feeRate = 0.07`, **rebate share 20%** (`rebateRate=0.2`, matches live `feeSchedule`). Sports–Tech 25%. Geopolitics fee-free.

**Every existing test created the directory in its own fixture.** `root = tmp_path / "project";

the bug is "nothing creates X", assert on an X that has deliberately never been created, and say
so in the test:

distribution. A fact term that is a rare phrase ("byte-identical prefix") costs nothing. A fact
term that is a common English word quietly makes every ordinary document mentioning it
unusable, and the shortfall is invisible in an aggregate.

rate, 1.00 for a ratio. Real data rarely hits the null value to four decimals. When it does, check
that the input exists before believing the result.

⚠️ **A partial failure is worse than a total one.** If the join fails for some rows only, those get
zeroed features while the rest are real, which manufactures a split in every affected feature
rather than flattening it. Total failure at least looks like nothing; partial failure looks like a
finding.

**A review-prompted fix is HIGHER risk than the original, not lower**, because it ships with the

introduced by the previous round's repair, two of them mine in consecutive turns. In a lock fix,

`huggingface_hub.utils._http.get_session()` returns `_GLOBAL_CLIENT` whenever it is not `None`,
**without checking `is_closed`**. So once that client is closed by anything other than
`close_session()`, every hub call in the process fails for the interpreter's lifetime.
`close_session()` is safe by contrast, it sets `_GLOBAL_CLIENT = None` BEFORE closing, so the
next call rebuilds.

⚠️ There are exactly TWO routes to `ClientState.CLOSED`, and the second is the trap:

Client.close()      # guarded
    Client.__exit__()   # sets self._state = ClientState.CLOSED DIRECTLY, never calls close()

So `with get_session() as c:`, ordinary, correct-looking httpx usage, poisons the module
permanently, and **monkeypatching `close()` to audit for it detects nothing**.

`tests/test_site_vendor_disclosure.py` is what makes it survive an ordinary edit, since the
leaderboard is generated but the four pages are not. It scans everything under `site/` for the
undisclosed names and for adjacent brands (Graphiti, FalkorDB, Letta, MemGPT), and it matches
**substrings, not word boundaries**. That was a real defect in my first version, caught in
review and measured both ways: a word-boundary match on "zep" misses `getzep.com`, and one on
"mem0" misses `mem0ai`, which are the two shapes a leak actually takes, a link and a package
name. A disclosure guard should over-match, because a false positive costs one rephrased
sentence and a miss costs a published name. Mutation-tested five ways.

**How to apply:**
- Define the matched phrase **once** as a named constant and reference it from every parse site, so
  alternations cannot drift apart.
- Accept the known wordings via alternation rather than pinning the dependency version — pinning
  makes the package unusable alongside newer installs.
- Add a guard test that runs the real upstream tool and asserts its output still matches. A rename
  then fails the suite loudly instead of silently turning every confirmation into an escalation.
- When local is green and CI is red, **reconstruct CI's environment locally**. A version skew you
  cannot see is the most likely cause, and reproducing beats reasoning.

baseline_items.text:
# Restore drill database boundary

The scheduled Aurora restore drill is a database recovery check. The validator discovers every
public table with a `tenant_id` column and requires forced row level security, a tenant policy, and
`SELECT` for the serving role across that set. It still does not start the MCP application or make
an authenticated HTTP request through OIDC, authorization, rate limiting, retrieval, and response
serialization.

Keep operational documentation explicit about this boundary until a separate application smoke
task is wired to the restored cluster.

# Restore drill database boundary

The scheduled Aurora restore drill is a database recovery check. The validator discovers every
public table with a `tenant_id` column and requires forced row level security, a tenant policy, and
`SELECT` for the serving role across that set. It still does not start the MCP application or make
an authenticated HTTP request through OIDC, authorization, rate limiting, retrieval, and response
serialization.

Keep operational documentation explicit about this boundary until a separate application smoke
task is wired to the restored cluster.

# Restore checksum validation is bounded by default

The Aurora restore drill hashes at most 10,000 rows per validated table by default, ordered by
the primary key of `recall_chunks_v1` or `recall_generations`. The receipt records the mode, row
bound, and per table durations. This keeps checksum work bounded as the corpus grows, but it can
miss corruption outside the deterministic prefix. Set `RECALL_RESTORE_CHECKSUM_MODE=full` for an
explicit high assurance drill that hashes every visible row. Expected checksums must be generated
with the same mode and bound. The change was made in commit `7c04f8bd` after the restore review
identified full table hashing as a possible RTO cost.

# Restore drill database boundary

The scheduled Aurora restore drill is a database recovery check. The validator discovers every
public table with a `tenant_id` column and requires forced row level security, a tenant policy, and
`SELECT` for the serving role across that set. It still does not start the MCP application or make
an authenticated HTTP request through OIDC, authorization, rate limiting, retrieval, and response
serialization.

Keep operational documentation explicit about this boundary until a separate application smoke
task is wired to the restored cluster.

```
elif (any(np.iscomplex(system.poles))
```

## Interpretazione SKIP

Se `skip > 0` significa che uno dei check ha incontrato una schema mismatch. Non è un failure ma **un segnale che la codebase si è mossa e audit/d*.py è da aggiornare**. Monta la fix.

⛔ **Do NOT pre-apply the schema to your fresh container. The fixtures provision it, at dim 64.**
2026-08-14 I ran `schema apply` on a new container "to get it ready"; it created
`recall_chunks_v1` at the default **vector(384)** while `make_store(64)` wants 64, and every
DB-touching test errored: **4533 errors, 12 skipped**, in a 677s run. It reads exactly like a
catastrophic regression and is entirely self-inflicted. The tell is in the numbers before the
traceback: 12 skipped (not ~22) with thousands of ERRORS rather than failures means collection-
or fixture-level breakage, not your change. Start the container, wait for `pg_isready`, and run
pytest, nothing else. The error to recognise is
`SchemaIncompatible: recall_chunks_v1 uses vector(384), requested dimension is 64`.

**How to apply:**
1. Quando una query `db_query_ro` ritorna `permission denied for table X`, **non** concludere "table assente". Verifica prima con `SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name='X'`.
2. Dopo CREATE TABLE in qualsiasi migration nuova, **includere** nella stessa migration:
   ```sql
   GRANT SELECT ON <new_table> TO qwen_ro;
   GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON <new_table> TO sentiment;
   ```
3. Per audit retroattivo periodico: `SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables t WHERE table_schema='public' AND NOT has_table_privilege('qwen_ro', table_schema||'.'||table_name, 'SELECT')`.
4. Considerare `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO qwen_ro` (default per future table) come fix permanente — discutere con root

**`RECALL_OIDC_SUBJECT_TENANTS` CONSTRAINS the tenant claim, it does not SUPPLY it.** I assumed it
let the deployment name the tenant and skip the claim. It does not: the token must still carry
`tenant`, and the binding then refuses a subject not bound to it. That is the configuration to
prefer over `RECALL_OIDC_TRUST_TENANT_CLAIM` (the IdP asserts, the deployment constrains), but it
means the IdP must emit the claim — and on Keycloak 24+ that additionally needs **unmanaged
attributes enabled on the realm's user profile**, or the attribute is silently dropped and the
token carries `tenant: null`.

`RECALL_OIDC_SUBJECT_TENANTS=sub:tenant,...` pins the mapping; a bound subject naming another
**provisioned** tenant is refused `subject_tenant_mismatch` on a genuine signed token. Checked
after the signature (else it enumerates subjects). The tenant is everything after the **LAST**
colon, so a k8s `system:serviceaccount:ns:sa` subject is bindable; a *forgotten* tenant is caught
by the allowed_tenants cross-check, not by the parser.

⚠️ **BREAKING: an OIDC deployment now refuses to boot until it answers.** Either pin the map, or
`RECALL_OIDC_TRUST_TENANT_CLAIM=1`. No default, because a default here is a fail-open.
